verdicts.evidence: The bottom-up build double-counts the receipts-to-outlay wedge twice over. (1) The ANPA $55m national newspaper figure is already an expenditure measure, not a Census receipts measure: for 1919 Galbi's sheet carries Census newspaper receipts 373.5 against ANPA national+local 500, with Coen-basis outlay at 567.2, so ANPA sits above receipts and needs at most a 1.13 uplift, not 1.52. The record's own e1-scale-012 treats the companion ANPA figure ($220m local) as outlay and does NOT scale it - the two claims handle the same ANPA table inconsistently. (2) Galbi does not scale Census 'other periodicals' at all (1919: Census 154.8, est. 154.8), yet the record scales $71.6m by 1.52. (3) HSUS's own source note for T 444 states 'The data include the cost of preparation', so the 1.52 factor is already preparation-inclusive; the method then adds preparation a second time to move $210m to $250-270m. Removing the double counts: unscaled 55 + 71.6 + 25 = $151.6m (12.6% of $1,200m); most generous defensible scaling 62 + 108.7 + 25 = $196m (16.3%). Nothing in the build reaches 22%.

new.method: Bottom-up on the 1914 benchmark of $1,100-1,302m. Components on a consistent expenditure basis: ANPA national newspaper space $55m (already an expenditure measure; at most a 1.13 uplift to Coen basis, giving $55-62m); Census non-newspaper periodicals $71.6m receipts, taken 70-100 percent national and left unscaled to $109m scaled, giving $50-109m; national outdoor and streetcar $15-40m. Total $150-211m against $1,100-1,302m = 11.5-19.2 percent. Preparation is NOT added separately because the Coen/HSUS total-outlay basis already includes it (HSUS chapter T source note for T 444-471).

verdicts.reason: The receipts-to-outlay wedge is applied to figures that are already on or near an outlay basis, and preparation is then added a second time on top of a preparation-inclusive factor. verdicts.evidence: The load-bearing step - interpolating $300m of 1920 direct mail back to '$200-250m' for 1914 - fails three independent cross-checks. (1) Share of total: $300m against Coen's 1920 total of $2,480m is 12.1 percent, against HSUS T 444's $2,935m it is 10.2 percent; applying either share to 1914 gives about $133m, not $200-250m. (2) Price level: the CPI roughly doubled 1914-1920, so $300m of 1920 direct mail is about $150m at 1914 prices for the same real volume, and real volume grew over the period, so the 1914 nominal figure must sit well under $150m on that route. (3) Upper bound from the next observed year: I read HSUS series T 464 off p. 857 and direct mail in 1935 was $282m against a T 444 total of $1,690m, i.e. 16.7 percent - a Depression-elevated share. The defensible 1914 band is therefore roughly 10-17 percent of total, or $120-190m, not $200-250m. Rebuilding the record's own components with that: 120-190 (direct mail) + 30-45 (mail-order keyed print) + 30-50 (patent medicine keyed press) + 40-70 (premiums, samples, novelties) = $220-355m, or 18.3-29.6 percent of $1,200m. Central lands near 24, not 32, and the superlative fails: at 24 percent direct response is statistically indistinguishable from local retail at 23 percent.

old.statement: Direct-response money ... was roughly 32 percent of total US advertising outlay at the 1914 benchmark, the single largest money type in the era.

new.statement: Direct-response money - catalogues, direct mail, and keyed print advertising bought by mail-order houses and patent-medicine makers - was roughly 24 percent of total US advertising outlay at the 1914 benchmark, comparable in size to local retail and the largest or joint-largest money type in the era.
new.unit: percent of total US advertising outlay
new.method: Direct mail and catalogues put at about $300m in 1920 (1926 Britannica). Back-cast three ways rather than one: direct mail was 10.2-12.1 percent of the 1920 total (Coen $2,480m / HSUS $2,935m) and 16.7 percent of the 1935 total (HSUS T 464 $282m over T 444 $1,690m), and the price level roughly doubled 1914-1920; the resulting 1914 band is $120-190m. Add mail-order houses' keyed print space $30-45m, patent-medicine keyed press $30-50m, and premiums, samples and novelties $40-70m. Total $220-355m against $1,100-1,302m. The superlative is dropped: at this level direct response and local retail are within the noise of each other.

verdicts.reason: The 1920-to-1914 back-cast was done on an assumed mail-volume growth path with no cross-check; three independent cross-checks (share of total in 1920, share of total in 1935, and the 1914-1920 price level) all put 1914 direct mail at $120-190m rather than $200-250m. The 'single largest money type' superlative does not survive the corrected magnitude.

verdicts.evidence: The 15 percent value is solid and is not in dispute: Horsky & Zeithammer quote Haase (1934, p. 3) that the uniform rate agents set was '15%', and separately establish that 15 percent was customary from the early 1890s and enforced by publisher recognition from 1893. What fails is the scope clause 'the only intermediary cut in the chain'. The cited evidence (Haase 1934) is explicitly about the 1918 rate - 'namely 15%, is one which we said to reflect costs of doing business in 1918' - which is inside era 2 by the record's own boundary note, and it says nothing about exclusivity. The record's own boundary note (4) concedes the industry-wide standardisation is a 1918 act; asserting an exclusive 1917 take rate on 1918 evidence over-reaches. Newspaper special representatives, who sold national space on behalf of publishers and were paid by publishers, were an established second intermediary layer by 1917; I could not source a rate for them within this run, which is precisely why the exclusivity clause should not be asserted.

old.statement: The agency layer's take rate at the end of the era was 15 percent of gross billings, the only intermediary cut in the chain; publishers retained the remaining 85 percent of the card price.

new.statement: The agency layer's customary take rate at the end of the era was 15 percent of gross billings, and publishers retained the remaining 85 percent of the card price. Fifteen percent was customary from the early 1890s and enforced from 1893 by publisher recognition; its industry-wide standardisation by the 4As is a 1918 act (era 2). The agency commission was the principal but not demonstrably the only intermediary cut: publishers also paid national special representatives, whose rate is not established here.

verdicts.evidence: I read HSUS series T 485-486 off p. 857 directly and it starts in 1928, not 1936 as the method's framing implies, so more evidence was available than the method used. Every anchor the method cites checks out (1936 265,475/1,380,121 = 19.24 percent; 1938 20.81; 1940 20.72). But the fuller series undercuts the argument used to push 1914 down. Classified's share of 52-city linage was 19.19 percent in 1928, 18.21 in 1929, 18.07 in 1930, 18.51 in 1933, 19.24 in 1936, 20.81 in 1938 - i.e. it sat in a tight 18-21 percent band while total linage collapsed 44 percent from 1929 to 1933. A share that stable through the worst demand shock of the century is weak support for 'the classified boom is a 1920s phenomenon, so the pre-WWI share is materially lower'; that remains an assumption with no evidence behind it. The stated ci80 upper bound of 18 sits below every single observation in the only series that exists (minimum 18.07). Under an honest interval test, the band must at least admit the possibility that 1914 was at the 1928-40 level.

Anchored on the earliest measured split: classified was 18-21 percent of newspaper linage in 52 cities across every year of 1928-1941 (Historical Statistics series T 485-486: 1928 345,835/1,802,482 = 19.2%; 1930 18.1%; 1933 18.5%; 1936 19.2%; 1938 20.8%; 1940 20.7%), a band that held through a 44 percent collapse in total linage. Classified is argued to be a smaller share pre-WWI because help-wanted, autos and real estate classified grew in the 1920s, and because the claim is about revenue rather than linage; but neither argument is evidenced, so the interval's upper bound is set at the observed 1928-40 level rather than below it. Cross-check: a 7-21 percent band on the Census 1914 newspaper receipts of $184.0m gives $13-39m, inside the ANPA 'local incl. classified' envelope of $220m for 1915.
